query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, the formation of a stable, adherent oxide film on FeNiCrCoCu coatings is the dominant mechanism controlling wear resistance. The multicomponent composition encourages an oxide layer that reduces direct metal-on-metal contact, thereby lowering wear.
generation.material_initial_state: Baseline is an equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating (deposited on a representative steel substrate) evaluated at near-room-temperature conditions with minimal oxide formation.
generation.intervention: Vary the test environment (ambient air versus inert atmosphere) and raise the temperature from room temperature to 800 °C, maintaining the baseline composition and coating thickness. Compare wear behavior and oxide-layer development under both conditions.
generation.conditions: Conduct pin-on-disk wear tests from 25 °C to 800 °C at moderate loads (e.g., 5–15 N) for prescribed sliding distances in air and in an inert gas environment such as argon.
generation.structural_mediator: A cohesive, thermally grown oxide scale forming on the coating surface during high-temperature operation in air.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated oxidation in air develops a protective oxide scale that reduces frictional contact and mitigates wear. In contrast, in an inert atmosphere that inhibits oxide formation, wear remains higher at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under air at 500–800 °C, the wear volume loss and friction coefficient should decrease by at least 20–30% compared to the baseline/room-temperature condition due to the oxide scale. In an inert environment where this scale does not form, wear rates will be higher at elevated temperature.
generation.baseline: Room-temperature wear performance of as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coatings in air, with only minor oxide products on the surface.
generation.boundary: Temperatures spanning from room temperature to about 800 °C and moderate normal loads. Behavior above 800 °C or under extreme loading/unusual environments remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The nature, adherence, and protective effect of the forming oxide scale may vary based on small composition differences and substrate-coating metallurgical interactions, complicating extrapolation to conditions beyond 800 °C.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical FeNiCrCoCu coatings on steel substrates. Perform systematic tribological tests from room temperature to 800 °C in both air and inert atmospheres. After testing, assess the presence and morphology of any oxide layers on worn surfaces via SEM, EDS, and XRD.
measurements: Wear volume or depth across temperature range
Coefficient of friction under air vs. inert environments
Thickness and composition of any oxide scales formed (via microstructural and chemical analyses)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant oxide layer is detected in air while wear is still reduced at elevated temperatures, or if a similarly low wear rate occurs in an inert environment where oxidation is suppressed, then the hypothesis would be invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: High hardness and good wear resistance have been revealed for the high-entropy alloy (HEA) system AlCoCrFeNiTi, confirming the potential for surface protection applications. Detailed studies to investigate the microstructure and phase formation have been carried out using different production routes. Powder metallurgical technologies allow for much higher flexibility in the customisation of materials compared to casting processes. Particularly, spark plasma sintering (SPS) enables the fast processing of the feedstock, the suppression of grain coarsening and the production of samples with a low porosity. Furthermore, solid lubricants can be incorporated for the improvement of wear resistance and the reduction of the coefficient of friction (COF). This study focuses on the production of AlCoCrFeNiTi composites comprising solid lubricants. Bulk materials with a MoS2 content of up to 15 wt % were produced. The wear resistance and COF were investigated in detail under sliding wear conditions in ball-on-disk tests at room temperature and elevated temperature. An influence of the test temperature on the wear behaviour under reciprocating wear conditions was observed. After completing the tests, the wear depth and average COF were determined. The results from ambient temperature up to 900 °C under atmospherical conditions are summarised in Figure 4. With an increase in temperature from room temperature to 500 °C, a slight increase in the wear depth occurs, indicating a reduced wear resistance. A further increase in test temperature results in a slight decrease in the wear depth. For the wear investigations at 800 °C, a distinct reduction in wear depth occurs. The highest wear resistance was proven for the test conducted at the highest temperature of 900 °C. Furthermore, the influence of the temperature on the average COF was investigated. With an increase in temperature up to 800 °C, the COF only slightly decreases. A high standard deviation occurs for all of these measurements. The lowest COF was measured for the highest test temperature of 900 °C, with an average value of 0.85.
